question: NPC: What shape should a network take?
intro: I'm Tariq, the Beacon-Courier. Before anyone pulls a cable, someone decides which boxes connect to which, and that shape decides how much one broken link can cost you. Changing it later can mean re-cabling a building, so it pays to choose well at the start. Let's begin with the simplest shape there is, the one in every wiring closet.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.4; node[shape=box]; hq[label="HQ (hub)", color="#ffb300", fontcolor="#ffd86b"]; b1[label="branch 1"]; b2[label="branch 2"]; b3[label="branch 3"]; b4[label="branch 4"]; hq--b1; hq--b2; hq--b3; hq--b4; }
figure.alt: A box labeled HQ, the hub, in the middle with four lines out to branch 1, 2, 3 and 4. The branches have no lines between them.
figure.caption: hub-and-spoke: one link per branch

beats.say: In a **star**, every device cables to one central device: each PC in a closet plugs into the same switch.
Across a WAN the same shape is called **hub-and-spoke**: each branch has one link, to headquarters, the hub.

steps.say: In a **star**, every device cables to one central device: each PC in a closet plugs into the same switch. Across a WAN the same shape is called **hub-and-spoke**: each branch has one link, to headquarters, the hub.

check.prompt: Five branches each link only to headquarters. A file goes from branch 2 to branch 4. What path does it take?
check.answer: Branch 2 to headquarters, then on to branch 4
wrong: Straight from branch 2 to branch 4
Around every branch in turn until it arrives
check.why: Spokes have no links between them, so spoke-to-spoke traffic always crosses the hub. That is the price of needing only one link per branch, and it makes the hub a **single point of failure**: lose it and every branch is cut off from the rest.

figure.dot: graph { nodesep=0.7; ranksep=0.7; node[shape=box]; a[label="site A"]; b[label="site B"]; c[label="site C"]; d[label="site D"]; a--b; a--c; a--d; b--c; b--d; c--d; }
figure.alt: Four sites, A to D, with a line between every pair of them: six lines in all.
figure.caption: a full mesh of four sites

beats.say: A **mesh** links sites directly. In a **full mesh** every site links to every other, so no single failure cuts anyone off.
The bill grows fast, as the table shows.

beats.code:
n sites: n - 1 links each
link = two ends, so
  links = n x (n - 1) / 2
4 sites: 4 x 3 / 2 = 6

beats.say: A **partial mesh** keeps only the links that earn their cost, such as one between two data centers.

steps.say: A **mesh** links sites directly. In a **full mesh** every site links to every other, so no single failure cuts anyone off. The bill grows fast, as the table shows. A **partial mesh** keeps only the links that earn their cost, such as one between two data centers.

check.prompt: A full mesh joins 6 sites. How many links does it need?
check.why: Each of the 6 sites has 5 links, which counts 30 link-ends; every link has two ends, so the mesh has 15 links. Hub-and-spoke would join the same 6 sites with 5.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.3; ranksep="0.8 equally"; subgraph cluster_core { label="core"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; {rank=same; c1[label="core-1"]; c2[label="core-2"];} } subgraph cluster_dist { label="distribution"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; {rank=same; d1[label="dist-1"]; d2[label="dist-2"]; d1--d2[style=invis];} } subgraph cluster_acc { label="access"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; {rank=same; a1[label="acc-1"]; a2[label="acc-2"]; a3[label="acc-3"]; a4[label="acc-4"]; a1--a2--a3--a4[style=invis];} } c1--c2; c1--d1; c1--d2; c2--d1; c2--d2; d1--a1; d1--a2; d2--a3; d2--a4; }
figure.alt: Three dashed bands stacked top to bottom: two core switches linked to each other and to both distribution switches, and each distribution switch linked to two of four access switches.
figure.caption: a three-tier campus

beats.say: In a **three-tier** campus, the **access** layer is where PCs, phones and access points plug in.
The **distribution** layer joins the access switches and applies policy, such as routing between VLANs.

steps.say: In a **three-tier** campus, the **access** layer is where PCs, phones and access points plug in. The **distribution** layer joins the access switches and applies policy, such as routing between VLANs.

beats.say: The **core** is a fast backbone joining the distribution blocks, kept free of heavy policy.
One building rarely needs a separate core. A **two-tier** design, also called a **collapsed core**, merges core and distribution.

steps.say: The **core** is a fast backbone joining the distribution blocks, kept free of heavy policy. One building rarely needs a separate core. A **two-tier** design, also called a **collapsed core**, merges core and distribution.

beats.say: Inside a data center, watch which way traffic flows.
Traffic entering or leaving, such as a remote worker reaching an internal server, is **north-south**.
Traffic between servers inside, such as one asking a storage server for a file, is **east-west**.
Modern applications are mostly east-west.

steps.say: Inside a data center, watch which way traffic flows. Traffic entering or leaving, such as a remote worker reaching an internal server, is **north-south**. Traffic between servers inside, such as one asking a storage server for a file, is **east-west**. Modern applications are mostly east-west.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.45; {rank=same; s1[label="spine-1"]; s2[label="spine-2"]; s1--s2[style=invis];} {rank=same; l1[label="leaf-1"]; l2[label="leaf-2"]; l3[label="leaf-3"]; l4[label="leaf-4"]; l1--l2--l3--l4[style=invis];} web[label="web\nserver"]; db[label="database"]; s1--l1; s1--l2; s1--l3; s1--l4; s2--l1; s2--l2; s2--l3; s2--l4; l1--web; l3--db; }
figure.alt: Two spine switches in a top row and four leaf switches below; each leaf has a line to both spines. A web server hangs off leaf-1 and a database off leaf-3.
figure.caption: spine-and-leaf

beats.say: **Spine-and-leaf** is built for that.
Servers plug into **leaf** switches, usually one per rack.
Every leaf links to every **spine**; leaves never link to each other, nor spines to spines.
A new spine adds bandwidth and a new leaf adds ports, each linked to every switch on the other tier.

steps.say: **Spine-and-leaf** is built for that. Servers plug into **leaf** switches, usually one per rack. Every leaf links to every **spine**; leaves never link to each other, nor spines to spines. A new spine adds bandwidth and a new leaf adds ports, each linked to every switch on the other tier.

check.prompt: The web server on leaf-1 queries the database on leaf-3. Which way does that flow, and which switches does it cross?
check.answer: East-west: leaf-1, one spine, then leaf-3
wrong: North-south: leaf-1, both spines, then leaf-3
East-west: leaf-1, leaf-2, then leaf-3
check.why: Server-to-server traffic inside the data center is east-west. Leaves have no links to each other, so every leaf-to-leaf path is leaf, spine, leaf: the same length whichever spine carries it, which keeps latency predictable.

outro: First, Captain Doran wants every branch's traffic to pass his firewall at headquarters. Choose the topology that does it with the fewest links.

question: Silverkeep Holdings links 12 branch offices. Captain Doran Kell wants all branch traffic, including branch-to-branch traffic, to pass the inspection firewall at headquarters, using as few WAN links as possible. Which topology fits?
correct: Hub-and-spoke
incorrect: Full mesh
Partial mesh
Spine-and-leaf
feedback: Hub-and-spoke gives each branch a single link to the hub, 12 links in all, and every branch-to-branch flow crosses headquarters, where the firewall sees it. A full mesh would need 12 × 11 ÷ 2, or 66, links and lets branches talk directly, bypassing the firewall; a partial mesh adds some of those bypass links. Spine-and-leaf is a switch fabric inside one data center, not a WAN design.

question: Captain Doran Kell is pricing a full-mesh WAN in which each of {{n}} sites has its own direct link to every other site. How many WAN links does the design need?
feedback_template: Each of the {{n}} sites links to the other {{others}}, and each link joins two sites, so the count is {{n}} × {{others}} ÷ 2, which is {{expected}} links. Hub-and-spoke would join the same sites with {{others}} links, which is why a full mesh is kept for a few critical sites.

question: Match each switch layer or role to what it does.

pairs.definition: Switches that PCs, phones and access points plug into
Switches that aggregate access switches and route between VLANs
A fast backbone joining distribution blocks, with little policy
One layer doing both backbone and aggregation at a small site
A data center rack switch that the servers plug into
A data center switch that every rack switch has a link to

feedback: In a three-tier campus, devices plug into access, distribution aggregates them and applies policy such as inter-VLAN routing, and the core just moves traffic fast. A collapsed core folds core and distribution together when one building does not justify both. In a data center fabric, servers plug into leaves, and every leaf links to every spine.

question: Captain Doran Kell is adding rack switch H to the data center fabric shown. Which cabling keeps every server-to-server path across the fabric the same length?
correct: One link from H to each of A, B and C
incorrect: One link from H to G, its neighbor in the lower row
One link from H to A, which already reaches B and C
Links to A, B and C, plus one to G for extra redundancy
feedback: The upper switches are spines and the lower ones leaves: every lower switch links to each upper one, and no two in a row are linked. A new leaf joins the same way, one link to every spine, so any two servers are leaf, spine, leaf apart. A link to G would create a leaf-to-leaf shortcut that only some paths can use, and a single uplink to A leaves H with one path and a single point of failure; spines are not linked to each other either.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.35; ranksep=0.6; {rank=same; A; B; C; A--B--C[style=invis];} {rank=same; D; E; F; G; H[label="H\n(new)", style="rounded,dashed", color="#ffb300", fontcolor="#ffd86b"]; D--E--F--G--H[style=invis];} A--D; A--E; A--F; A--G; B--D; B--E; B--F; B--G; C--D; C--E; C--F; C--G; }
figure.alt: Three switches lettered A to C sit in an upper row and four lettered D to G in a lower row. Each lower switch has one line to every upper switch, and no two switches in the same row are joined. A dashed, unconnected box H sits at the end of the lower row.
figure.caption: a fabric with one switch still to cable

question: A customer on the internet loading Silverkeep's web page creates {{1}} traffic, because it crosses the data center's edge. The web server then querying a database two racks away creates {{2}} traffic, which never leaves the data center.
feedback: North-south traffic enters or leaves the data center, between clients outside and servers inside. East-west traffic runs between servers inside it, and in modern applications it is usually the larger share, which is why fabrics like spine-and-leaf are designed around it and why an edge firewall alone cannot see it.

question: Which of the following are characteristics of a spine-and-leaf data center fabric?
correct: Every leaf switch has a link to every spine switch
Any two servers on different leaves are the same number of hops apart
Adding a spine adds bandwidth between all of the leaves
incorrect: Leaf switches link to each other so busy racks can share uplinks
Servers plug into the spines to get the shortest path to the core
feedback: Every leaf links to every spine, so any leaf-to-leaf path is leaf, spine, leaf, and a new spine adds one more equal path between every pair of leaves. Leaves do not link to each other; that would make some paths shorter than others. Servers plug into leaves, and the spines are the fabric's backbone, so there is no separate core above them to reach.

question: NPC: Who is each network for, and what runs on it?
intro: A stranger reading your website and an employee filing expenses both reach your servers, but you'd never let them reach the same ones. So an organization keeps separate networks for separate audiences and guards each one differently. The one your own staff use every day comes first.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.4; inet[label="internet", shape=ellipse]; fw[label="firewall"]; subgraph cluster_dmz { label="DMZ"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#ffb300"; fontcolor="#ffd86b"; web[label="web server"]; mail[label="mail relay"]; } subgraph cluster_in { label="internal LAN"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; pcs[label="staff PCs"]; hr[label="HR portal\n(intranet)"]; } inet--fw; fw--web; fw--mail; fw--pcs; fw--hr; }
figure.alt: The internet connects to one firewall, which has two dashed zones behind it: one holding a web server and a mail relay, the other holding staff PCs and the HR portal.
figure.caption: one firewall, two zones

beats.say: An **intranet** is a private set of services, such as the HR portal, for staff only.
An **extranet** opens a controlled slice to named outsiders, such as suppliers, who must sign in.
A **DMZ**, or screened subnet, is a buffer zone between the internet and the inside, for public-facing servers.

steps.say: An **intranet** is a private set of services, such as the HR portal, for staff only. An **extranet** opens a controlled slice to named outsiders, such as suppliers, who must sign in. A **DMZ**, or screened subnet, is a buffer zone between the internet and the inside, for public-facing servers.

check.prompt: A supplier signs in to check its own orders in Silverkeep's inventory system. What type of network is that?
check.answer: An extranet: named outsiders, signed in, limited access
wrong: An intranet: it reaches an internal system
A DMZ: it is open to anyone on the internet
check.why: An extranet extends a controlled part of internal services to authenticated partners. An intranet is for staff only, and a DMZ holds services meant for the general public.

beats.say: **IoT**, the Internet of Things, means everyday devices with a network connection, such as cameras and smart TVs.
Many ship with weak default passwords and are rarely patched.
So they get a VLAN of their own.

steps.say: **IoT**, the Internet of Things, means everyday devices with a network connection, such as cameras and smart TVs. Many ship with weak default passwords and are rarely patched. So they get a VLAN of their own.

check.prompt: A new smart TV in the boardroom still has its factory password. Where should it be connected?
check.answer: On the IoT VLAN, kept apart from staff PCs and servers
wrong: On the staff VLAN, so it can reach the file servers
In the DMZ, beside the public website
check.why: A weakly secured device belongs on a segment of its own, where a compromise cannot spread to staff machines. The DMZ is for servers the public must reach, not for internal gadgets.

beats.say: **Operational technology** (OT) runs physical things, such as valves and motors.
**SCADA**, supervisory control and data acquisition, is OT that supervises a widespread process.
A control center collects readings from remote controllers and sends commands back.
In OT, safety and availability come first: a careless reboot can halt a line.

steps.say: **Operational technology** (OT) runs physical things, such as valves and motors. **SCADA**, supervisory control and data acquisition, is OT that supervises a widespread process. A control center collects readings from remote controllers and sends commands back. In OT, safety and availability come first: a careless reboot can halt a line.

beats.say: An **air-gapped** network has no connection to any other network, wired or wireless.
Data crosses only on removable media, so the media become the thing to control.
A **wireless bridge** joins two wired networks over a radio link, such as across a road.

steps.say: An **air-gapped** network has no connection to any other network, wired or wireless. Data crosses only on removable media, so the media become the thing to control. A **wireless bridge** joins two wired networks over a radio link, such as across a road.

check.prompt: An air-gapped control network needs a firmware update from the vendor's website. How does it get there?
check.answer: Downloaded elsewhere, scanned, and carried in on approved media
wrong: Through a temporary VPN from the vendor
Over a wireless bridge from the office network
check.why: An air gap means no network path at all, temporary or wireless. Updates are fetched on a separate machine, checked, and carried across on controlled removable media, which is why media scanning is part of the design.

beats.say: A **content delivery network** (CDN) keeps copies of a site's content on **edge servers** in many cities.
Each request goes to a nearby edge, usually steered there by DNS.
On a **cache hit**, the edge already has the file and answers at once.

steps.say: A **content delivery network** (CDN) keeps copies of a site's content on **edge servers** in many cities. Each request goes to a nearby edge, usually steered there by DNS. On a **cache hit**, the edge already has the file and answers at once.

beats.say: On a **cache miss**, the edge fetches the file from the **origin**, the site's own server.
It keeps a copy, then serves it.
Users get lower latency, and the origin carries less load.
Pages built for one user, such as a shopping basket, still go to the origin.

steps.say: On a **cache miss**, the edge fetches the file from the **origin**, the site's own server. It keeps a copy, then serves it. Users get lower latency, and the origin carries less load. Pages built for one user, such as a shopping basket, still go to the origin.

check.prompt: The website's logo is changed at the origin, but users keep seeing the old one for an hour. Why?
check.answer: The edges serve their cached copy until it expires
wrong: The origin is still sending the old logo
DNS now sends users straight to the origin
check.why: Each cached copy has a **time to live** (TTL); until it expires, the edge serves it without asking the origin. To push a change at once, purge the cache or give the new file a new name.

outro: Next come six kinds of network and six descriptions. Match each type to the one that fits it.

question: Match each network type to its description.

pairs.definition: Internal services reachable only by the organization's own staff
A controlled share of internal services for signed-in partners
A screened zone for servers the public internet must reach
A network with no wired or wireless path to any other network
A radio link that joins two wired networks into one
Central supervision of a physical process spread over a wide area

feedback: Intranet and extranet differ in audience: staff only, versus named partners who sign in. A DMZ is for the public, kept apart from the inside. An air gap has no path at all, while a wireless bridge is a path, joining two sites by radio. SCADA is the operational technology that runs pipelines, grids and water networks from a control center.

question: Silverkeep is moving its public website onto a server of its own. Anyone on the internet must reach it, but if it is compromised it must not share a segment with staff PCs, and it must not sit outside every firewall. In which segment of the diagram should it go?
correct: A
incorrect: B
C
D
feedback: Segment A sits between the outer and inner firewalls: it is a DMZ. The outer firewall lets the internet reach the web server there, and the inner firewall keeps a compromised server from reaching staff PCs (B) or the camera VLAN (C). Segment D is in front of every firewall, so a server there would face the internet unfiltered.

figure.dot: graph { rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.25; inet[label="internet", shape=ellipse]; rtr[label="ISP router"]; D[label="segment D"]; fw1[label="outer firewall"]; A[label="segment A"]; fw2[label="inner firewall"]; B[label="segment B\nstaff PCs"]; C[label="segment C\ncameras"]; inet--rtr; rtr--D; D--fw1; fw1--A; A--fw2; fw2--B; fw2--C; }
figure.alt: A chain from the internet to an ISP router, then segment D, then an outer firewall, then segment A, then an inner firewall. Behind the inner firewall sit segment B with staff PCs and segment C with cameras.
figure.caption: four candidate segments

question: At a bottling plant, Brom proposes letting the production line's Windows control workstations install the monthly patch bundle automatically overnight, along with the office PCs. The OT engineer refuses. What is the BEST reason?
correct: A surprise reboot or untested patch can halt the line, so OT changes are tested and scheduled first
incorrect: Patches matter mainly for hosts that browse the web, which control workstations do not do
OT networks are air-gapped by definition, so the patch would have no way to reach them
SCADA protocols encrypt every command, so a control workstation has no exposure to patch
feedback: In OT, safety and availability come first: an automatic overnight reboot could stop production or leave a process in an unsafe state, so patches are tested against the control software and applied in a planned window. Unpatched OT hosts are still exposed, browsing or not, because malware spreads across networks and on removable media. OT is not air-gapped by definition, and many older SCADA protocols send commands with no encryption at all.

question: Aria Thorne puts the building's smart thermostats, badge readers and security cameras, many still on factory passwords, on a VLAN of their own. These everyday network-connected devices are collectively known as ___ devices.
correct: IoT
Internet of Things
feedback: IoT, the Internet of Things, covers ordinary devices with a network connection. They are numerous, often weakly secured and rarely patched, so they are segmented away from staff PCs and servers: a compromised camera should not be able to reach the file server.

question: A CDN delivers Silverkeep's product images. In one hour its edge servers receive {{req}} requests for them, with a cache hit ratio of {{hit}}%. Each cache miss is fetched from the origin server. How many requests reach the origin that hour?
feedback_template: Hits are answered by the edge; only misses go back to the origin. The misses are the other {{missp}}% of {{req}} requests, which is {{expected}}. The origin handles a small fraction of the traffic, and most users are answered by a nearby edge.

question: NPC: How can one physical server run many machines?
intro: One physical server in a data center can carry dozens of servers at once, and each behaves as if it had the hardware to itself. That's why a new server, or even a new firewall, can be running in minutes instead of arriving in a box. All of it rests on one piece of sharing software.

beats.say: A **hypervisor** lets one physical host run many **virtual machines** (VMs).
Each VM has its own **guest OS**, the operating system inside it, and the hypervisor keeps the VMs isolated.

steps.say: A **hypervisor** lets one physical host run many **virtual machines** (VMs). Each VM has its own **guest OS**, the operating system inside it, and the hypervisor keeps the VMs isolated.

beats.say: A **Type 1**, or **bare-metal**, hypervisor runs straight on the hardware, as data center hosts do.
A **Type 2**, or **hosted**, hypervisor runs as an application on a desktop operating system.
That suits a lab on a laptop.

steps.say: A **Type 1**, or **bare-metal**, hypervisor runs straight on the hardware, as data center hosts do. A **Type 2**, or **hosted**, hypervisor runs as an application on a desktop operating system. That suits a lab on a laptop.

check.prompt: Brom wants to try a firewall image on his Windows laptop without wiping it. Which hypervisor fits?
check.answer: Type 2, running as an application on Windows
wrong: Type 1, installed in place of Windows
Neither: a firewall image cannot run in a VM
check.why: A hosted hypervisor runs on top of the existing OS, so the laptop stays as it is. A bare-metal one would replace Windows, and virtual firewalls are an everyday use of VMs.

beats.say: Inside the host, a **virtual switch** connects the VMs to each other.
Through the host's physical network cards, it also reaches the real network.

steps.say: Inside the host, a **virtual switch** connects the VMs to each other. Through the host's physical network cards, it also reaches the real network.

figure.dot: digraph { rankdir=BT; nodesep=0.2; ranksep=0.2; edge[arrowhead=none]; subgraph cluster_vm { label="virtual machines"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; hw1[label="hardware"]; hv[label="hypervisor"]; g1[label="guest OS"]; g2[label="guest OS"]; v1[label="app"]; v2[label="app"]; hw1->hv; hv->g1; hv->g2; g1->v1; g2->v2; } subgraph cluster_ct { label="containers"; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#5aaa5a"; fontcolor="#c8ffb0"; hw2[label="hardware"]; os[label="host OS\nkernel", color="#7CFC00", fontcolor="#7CFC00"]; eng[label="container\nengine"]; k1[label="app + libs"]; k2[label="app + libs"]; hw2->os; os->eng; eng->k1; eng->k2; } }
figure.alt: Two stacks side by side. Left: hardware, then a hypervisor, then two guest OS boxes each topped by an app. Right: hardware, then a highlighted host OS kernel, then a container engine topped by two app-plus-libraries boxes.
figure.caption: two ways to share one machine

beats.say: A **container** packages an application with its libraries.
It shares the host's operating system **kernel**, the core of the OS.
With no guest OS to boot, it is small, starts in seconds, and runs the same on a laptop as in the cloud.

steps.say: A **container** packages an application with its libraries. It shares the host's operating system **kernel**, the core of the OS. With no guest OS to boot, it is small, starts in seconds, and runs the same on a laptop as in the cloud.

beats.say: **Microservices** split one big application into small services, each doing one job, such as login or search.
They talk to each other over the network through **APIs**, interfaces built for programs.
Each usually runs in containers of its own.

steps.say: **Microservices** split one big application into small services, each doing one job, such as login or search. They talk to each other over the network through **APIs**, interfaces built for programs. Each usually runs in containers of its own.

check.prompt: During a sale only the checkout service is overloaded. In a microservices design, what is scaled out?
check.answer: Just checkout, by running more of its containers
wrong: The whole application, onto bigger VMs
Every service equally, to keep versions in step
check.why: Each microservice is deployed and scaled on its own, so you add containers only where the load is. A **monolith**, one application in one piece, would have to be scaled whole.

beats.say: **Network function virtualization** (NFV) does the same for network gear.
A firewall or router can run as software, a **virtual network function** (VNF), on an ordinary server.
A new branch firewall is a VM deployed in minutes, not an appliance to order, ship and rack.

steps.say: **Network function virtualization** (NFV) does the same for network gear. A firewall or router can run as software, a **virtual network function** (VNF), on an ordinary server. A new branch firewall is a VM deployed in minutes, not an appliance to order, ship and rack.

check.prompt: A virtual router and a virtual firewall run on the same host. The host's power supply fails. What happens?
check.answer: Both functions go down together
wrong: Only one fails; VNFs fail one at a time
Neither fails; the hypervisor keeps them in memory
check.why: Every VM on a host shares its hardware, so one host failure takes them all down. NFV designs run functions on clusters of hosts, so a failed host's VMs restart on another.

outro: Next, two ways of packaging a workload are described side by side. Fill in which is which.

question: A {{1}} carries its own guest operating system and boots on a hypervisor, while a {{2}} shares the host's kernel, carries only its app and libraries, and starts in seconds.
feedback: A virtual machine is a whole computer in software, guest OS included, which makes it heavier but strongly isolated. A container shares the host kernel and packages just the application and its libraries, so it is light and quick to start; that is why microservices usually run in containers.

question: Zinna Arc is building hosts for Silverkeep's new server cluster. The virtualization layer must run directly on each server's hardware, with no desktop operating system underneath it. What does she install?
correct: A Type 1 hypervisor
incorrect: A Type 2 hypervisor
A container engine
A virtual switch
feedback: A Type 1, bare-metal, hypervisor runs on the hardware itself, so there is no host OS underneath to patch or to compete for resources. A Type 2 hypervisor runs on top of a desktop OS, which suits a lab laptop, not a cluster. A container engine needs a host OS whose kernel its containers share, and a virtual switch is only the networking inside a hypervisor.

question: Silverkeep's developers are splitting a monolithic ordering application into microservices that run in containers. Which statements about the new design are accurate?
correct: Each service can be updated without redeploying the others
Containers on one host share that host's operating system kernel
The services talk to each other over the network through APIs
incorrect: Each container boots a guest operating system of its own, as a VM does
Scaling the busiest service also means scaling the rest, as with the monolith
Containers need a Type 2 hypervisor installed on every host
feedback: Microservices are independent: each is deployed, updated and scaled on its own, and they cooperate over the network through APIs. Containers share the host's kernel, which is what makes them light; booting a guest OS is what a VM does. Containers run on a host OS through a container engine, with or without a hypervisor underneath, so no Type 2 hypervisor is needed.

question: Marketstone Exchange's provider offers to replace the branch's physical router, firewall and WAN optimizer with software versions of each, running as VMs on one standard server. What is this approach called?
correct: Network function virtualization
incorrect: Microservices architecture
Containerization of the appliances
Hosted (Type 2) virtualization
feedback: Running network appliances as virtual network functions on ordinary servers is NFV. The VNFs do sit on a hypervisor, but the name for replacing the boxes with software is NFV. Microservices split one application into small services, containerization packages apps that share a kernel, and a Type 2 hypervisor is the desktop kind, not what a branch server would run.

question: NPC: What are you really renting when you use the cloud?

beats.say: A **public cloud** is open to anyone who pays.
It is **multitenant**: many customers, or **tenants**, share its hosts, kept apart by software.

steps.say: A **public cloud** is open to anyone who pays. It is **multitenant**: many customers, or **tenants**, share its hosts, kept apart by software.

public    anyone who pays

community a defined group
hybrid    mixed models

beats.say: A **private cloud** serves one organization only. A **community cloud** is shared by a defined group, such as hospitals.
A **hybrid cloud** joins two or more.

wrong: Hybrid
Public

In **PaaS**, platform as a service, the provider also runs the OS. You deploy only code.
In **SaaS**, software as a service, you just use the finished app and manage your users and data.

check.answer: You do: in IaaS the guest OS is yours
wrong: The provider: it owns the hardware
Nobody: cloud VMs patch themselves

beats.say: **Scalability** is the ability to add capacity as demand grows.
You **scale up** to a bigger VM, or **scale out** to more VMs.
**Elasticity** adds two things: it is automatic, and it works in both directions.

check.prompt: Under that rule, load reaches 1,800 requests per second. How many web servers run?
check.why: 1,800 ÷ 500 is 3.6, and a server cannot be part-launched, so the group rounds up to 4. When load falls back to 900, elasticity shrinks it to 2.

outro: First come the four ways a cloud can be deployed. Match each model to its description.

question: Match each cloud deployment model to its description.

pairs.definition: A provider's shared hosts, open to any paying customer
Infrastructure for one organization only, on or off its premises
Infrastructure shared only by organizations with common needs
Two or more models joined so workloads can move between them

feedback: Public clouds are multitenant and open to all; private clouds serve one organization, whether in its own building or hosted; community clouds are shared by a defined group such as hospitals or agencies; hybrid clouds join two or more of these into one working whole.

question: Thornwood Clinic uses three cloud services. On its rented VMs it patches the operating system itself: that is {{1}}. For its booking app it uploads only code, and the provider runs the OS and runtime: that is {{2}}. For email its staff just sign in, and the clinic manages only users: that is {{3}}.
feedback: The service models differ in where the provider's job stops. In IaaS it stops at the hypervisor and the customer runs the OS and up; in PaaS the provider runs the OS and runtime and the customer brings code; in SaaS the provider runs the whole application and the customer manages only users and data.

question: An autoscaling group runs enough web servers that none handles more than {{cap}} requests per second. During a sale, load reaches {{load}} requests per second. How many web servers does the group run?
feedback_template: {{load}} ÷ {{cap}} rounds up to {{expected}}: you cannot launch part of a server, and rounding down would push every server past its limit. When the sale ends, elasticity releases the extra servers automatically; a design that could grow but never shrank would be scalable, not elastic.

question: Silverkeep's VMs run on physical hosts shared with other customers' VMs, kept apart in software: that is {{1}}. The platform can add capacity as the business grows: that is {{2}}. It adds servers on its own when morning load arrives and releases them at night: that is {{3}}.
feedback: Multitenancy is many customers on shared infrastructure, isolated from each other. Scalability is the capacity to grow; elasticity is growing and shrinking automatically with demand, which is what makes pay-per-use pricing work.

question: NPC: How does your network reach into the cloud?
intro: Once a workload runs in the cloud, it still has to talk to your offices and to other cloud networks. There are three ways in, each with a different price in money, time and steadiness, and one connection that doesn't behave the way you'd expect.

beats.say: Your network in the cloud is a **virtual private cloud** (VPC): a private, isolated slice of the provider's network.
A site-to-site **VPN** is an encrypted tunnel from your data center across the internet: cheap and quick, but only as steady as the internet.

steps.say: Your network in the cloud is a **virtual private cloud** (VPC): a private, isolated slice of the provider's network. A site-to-site **VPN** is an encrypted tunnel from your data center across the internet: cheap and quick, but only as steady as the internet.

beats.say: A **cloud interconnect** is a dedicated private circuit into the provider's network, bypassing the internet.
It gives steady bandwidth and latency, but costs more and can take weeks to set up.

steps.say: A **cloud interconnect** is a dedicated private circuit into the provider's network, bypassing the internet. It gives steady bandwidth and latency, but costs more and can take weeks to set up.

beats.say: **Peering** joins two VPCs so they route to each other privately.
It is **non-transitive**: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C through B.

steps.say: **Peering** joins two VPCs so they route to each other privately. It is **non-transitive**: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C through B.

check.prompt: VPC A must reach VPC C in that layout. What is the fix?
check.answer: Peer A with C, or attach all three to a transit hub
wrong: Turn on routing in B so it forwards for its peers
Nothing: B already relays traffic between its peers
check.why: A peering carries traffic only between the two networks it joins; B will not forward for A. Either add a direct A-to-C peering, or attach every VPC to a **transit gateway**, a hub that does route between them: hub-and-spoke again.

outro: Next, a diagram shows every peering connection between Silverkeep's VPCs. Decide which networks the application can reach.

question: Zinna Arc's application runs in VPC P. The diagram shows every peering connection between Silverkeep's VPCs, and there is no transit hub. Which VPCs can the application reach privately?
correct: Q
S
incorrect: R
T
feedback: Peering is non-transitive: P reaches only the VPCs it is directly peered with, Q and S. R is peered with Q, and T with S, but neither Q nor S forwards traffic for P. To reach R and T, P needs peerings of its own with them, or the VPCs need a transit gateway.

question: Marketstone Exchange replicates trading data to its cloud VPC all day over a site-to-site VPN. The tunnel stays up, but latency swings whenever the internet is congested, and the auditors want the traffic kept off the internet. Which connectivity option fits?
correct: A cloud interconnect, a private circuit into the provider
incorrect: A second site-to-site VPN through another internet provider
A peering connection between the trading VPC and a second VPC
A client VPN installed on each of the trading workstations
feedback: A cloud interconnect is a dedicated private circuit from the customer's network into the provider's, bypassing the internet, with steady bandwidth and latency. A second VPN still rides the internet, peering joins two VPCs rather than reaching the data center, and a client VPN is for individual remote users.

question: NPC: How does software reshape a network without new cables?
intro: Moving a cable in a data center takes a ticket and a maintenance window, but the networks over those cables don't have to wait. Once software runs the network, you can lay a new network on top of the old one, or steer a whole WAN from one console. The first trick is carrying a LAN across a routed network.

beats.say: **VXLAN** carries Layer 2 across a Layer 3 network.
It wraps the original Ethernet frame whole in a VXLAN header, UDP port 4789, and a new outer IP header.
A **VTEP**, a VXLAN tunnel endpoint, does the wrapping and unwrapping.
The wrapper adds 50 bytes to each frame.

steps.say: **VXLAN** carries Layer 2 across a Layer 3 network. It wraps the original Ethernet frame whole in a VXLAN header, UDP port 4789, and a new outer IP header. A **VTEP**, a VXLAN tunnel endpoint, does the wrapping and unwrapping. The wrapper adds 50 bytes to each frame.

check.prompt: The wrapper adds 50 bytes to each frame, and the servers send standard 1,500-byte packets. What must the underlay's MTU, the largest packet its links will carry, be?
check.answer: At least 1,550 bytes
wrong: Exactly 1,500 bytes, matching the servers
At most 1,450 bytes, to leave room
check.why: Each outer packet is the inner packet plus 50 bytes of wrapping, so the underlay must carry 1,550 bytes, or full-size packets fragment or drop. VXLAN fabrics usually run **jumbo frames**, larger than 1,500 bytes, often around 9,000.

beats.say: The routed network the outer packets cross is the **underlay**.
The Layer 2 segments riding on it are the **overlay**.
A 24-bit **VNI** numbers each segment.

IDs
VLAN tag  4,094 (12-bit)
VXLAN VNI 16 million

beats.say: Stretch an overlay across two data centers and you get a **data center interconnect** (DCI): one segment at both sites.

steps.say: The routed network the outer packets cross is the **underlay**. The Layer 2 segments riding on it are the **overlay**. A 24-bit **VNI** numbers each segment. Stretch an overlay across two data centers and you get a **data center interconnect** (DCI): one segment at both sites.

check.prompt: A VM is live-migrated, moved while still running, from site 1 to site 2 across the DCI. What happens to its IP address?
check.answer: It keeps it: its subnet exists at both sites
wrong: It gets a new one from site 2's DHCP server
The VTEP rewrites it to a site 2 address
check.why: Because the segment is stretched, the VM lands in the same subnet with the same IP and gateway, so its sessions survive. Without the DCI it would need readdressing at the new site.

Its **data plane** forwards each packet using those tables.
The **management plane** is how you configure and monitor it.
**Software-defined networking** (SDN) moves the control plane into a central **controller**.

The management plane, which only logs it

check.prompt: A new branch has no MPLS service in its town, only broadband and LTE. Can it join the SD-WAN?
check.answer: Yes: the overlay runs over whatever links the site has
wrong: No: SD-WAN needs MPLS as its underlay
Only once its LTE link is converted to MPLS
check.why: Transport agnostic means the tunnels don't care what carries them. Many branches run SD-WAN over broadband, with LTE as the backup.

**Central policy management** means a rule written once reaches every site.
**Zero-touch provisioning** means anyone can plug in a new edge device, and it sets itself up.

outro: Next, two cloud tenants use the same VLAN number, yet their traffic never mixes. Name what keeps them apart.

question: Two tenants in Silverkeep's cloud both use VLAN 10 on their own VMs, yet their traffic never mixes across the fabric, because the VTEPs map each tenant's VLAN 10 to a different 24-bit ___.
correct: VNI
VXLAN Network Identifier
VXLAN network ID
VNID
VXLAN ID
feedback: The VNI, the VXLAN network identifier, sits in the 8-byte VXLAN header and names the segment a frame belongs to. Its 24 bits give 16,777,216 values, against the 12-bit VLAN ID's 4,096, of which 4,094 are usable.

question: A VM on host 1 sends a frame to a VM in the same VXLAN segment on host 2, in another rack. Arrange what happens, from first to last.
items: The VM sends an ordinary Ethernet frame to its virtual switch
The local VTEP looks up which remote VTEP serves the destination
The local VTEP wraps the frame in VXLAN, UDP and outer IP headers
The underlay routes the packet by its outer IP address
The remote VTEP strips the outer headers and delivers the frame
feedback: The VM knows nothing of VXLAN: it sends a normal frame. The local VTEP finds the remote VTEP for the destination MAC, encapsulates the frame, and hands it to the underlay, which routes on the outer IP header like any other packet. The remote VTEP decapsulates and delivers the original frame, untouched, to the destination VM.

question: Silverkeep has two data centers 30 km apart, joined by a routed IP link. Zinna Arc must let VMs live-migrate between them without changing their IP addresses. What should she deploy?
correct: VXLAN, stretching each segment across the routed link as a DCI
incorrect: 802.1Q trunking, carrying the VLAN tags across the routed link
VPC peering between the two data centers' server subnets
NFV, with a virtual router running at each data center
feedback: A DCI built on VXLAN wraps each Layer 2 frame in UDP and IP, so it crosses the routed link and the same segment exists at both sites; a migrated VM keeps its address. An 802.1Q tag lives in an Ethernet frame and does not survive a router hop. Peering connects cloud VPCs at Layer 3, and a virtual router routes between subnets rather than stretching one.

question: Match each SD-WAN feature to what it does.

pairs.definition: Recognizes each app's traffic and sends it down the path its policy names
Builds the same overlay over MPLS, broadband, LTE or satellite
Lets a new edge device configure itself by calling home when plugged in
Pushes one rule, written once on the controller, to every site

feedback: Application awareness is per-app path choice based on measured latency, loss and jitter. Transport agnosticism is the overlay's indifference to what carries it. Zero-touch provisioning removes the engineer from branch installs, and central policy management means a rule is written once and every edge receives it.

question: In a router, the {{1}} plane decides where traffic should go by building the routing table, while the {{2}} plane forwards each packet using that table. SDN moves the first of these into a central {{3}}.
feedback: The control plane thinks and the data plane forwards. In a traditional router both live in the box; SDN centralizes the control plane in a controller that programs every device's data plane through southbound APIs, which is what lets one console steer the whole network.

question: A new SD-WAN edge device arrives at Ember Forge Workshop. Arrange its zero-touch provisioning, from first to last.
items: The shop manager connects power and the internet cable
The device gets an address on its internet port by DHCP
It calls home to the controller and proves its identity by certificate
It downloads its configuration and the central policy
It builds tunnels to the other sites and starts forwarding
feedback: Zero-touch provisioning needs only power and a cable on site. The device needs an address before it can reach anything, then it contacts the controller and authenticates, so a stolen or fake box gets nothing. Only then does it receive its configuration and policy, and with those it builds its tunnels and joins the overlay.

question:
Silverkeep's SD-WAN controller pushes this central policy to Ember Forge Workshop, which has three links: MPLS, broadband internet and LTE. A link meets SLA, its service-level target, when latency is under 150 ms and loss under 1%. LTE is up and meets SLA in every row below. Hold means the traffic waits until an allowed link is back.

Voice: MPLS if it meets SLA; else broadband if it meets SLA; else LTE.
Card payments: MPLS whenever MPLS is up, whatever its SLA; else broadband; never LTE, so Hold if neither is up.
Office suite (SaaS): broadband, straight to the internet, while broadband is up; else MPLS.
Nightly backup: broadband while it is up; else Hold.

Choose the path for each row.
feedback: One site, four applications, four rules: that is application awareness. Voice takes the first link that meets SLA in the order MPLS, broadband, LTE, so 210 ms on MPLS sends it to broadband, and with MPLS down and broadband losing 3% it falls to LTE. Payments ignore SLA and stay on MPLS while it is up, even at 2% loss; with both wired links down the rule forbids LTE, so they hold. The office suite prefers broadband for its direct path to the internet and falls back to MPLS, while backups wait for broadband rather than load MPLS or the metered LTE link.

question: NPC: How do you manage a network with code?
intro: I'm Professor Flint. Type the same change into forty switches by hand and, somewhere around the twenty-third, you'll get one wrong without noticing. Programs don't get tired, so let them make the change, and keep a record of exactly what they were told. First, a program needs a way to talk to the device.

beats.say: An **API** is a door built for programs, not people.
**REST** is the common style: each thing has a URL, and HTTP methods act on it.

beats.code:
method  does
GET     reads
POST    creates
PUT     replaces
PATCH   changes part
DELETE  removes

beats.language: a REST call and its reply

beats.say: **SOAP** is older: each message is an XML document in an envelope.
**GraphQL** has one endpoint; the query is shaped like the answer.

steps.say: An **API** is a door built for programs, not people. **REST** is the common style: each thing has a URL, and HTTP methods act on it. **SOAP** is older: each message is an XML document in an envelope. **GraphQL** has one endpoint; the query is shaped like the answer.

check.prompt: A dashboard needs only the hostname and OS version of 500 switches, and the REST API returns dozens of fields for each. Which style lets it ask for just those two?
check.answer: GraphQL: the query lists only the fields it wants
wrong: SOAP: its envelope drops the fields it doesn't need
REST, by sending POST instead of GET
check.why: A GraphQL query names the fields to return, so each switch comes back with just two, and related data can come in the same request. REST returns whatever the resource holds, and SOAP is about strict XML contracts, not trimming replies.

beats.say: **Infrastructure as code** (IaC) keeps the network's intended state in files, such as VLANs and ACLs.
A tool reads the files and makes the devices match.
A **template** is a config with blanks, such as hostname and VLANs, filled in per site.

steps.say: **Infrastructure as code** (IaC) keeps the network's intended state in files, such as VLANs and ACLs. A tool reads the files and makes the devices match. A **template** is a config with blanks, such as hostname and VLANs, filled in per site.

check.prompt: Forty branch switches need the same baseline, but each has its own hostname and VLAN numbers. What do you write?
check.answer: One template, filled in from each site's variables
wrong: Forty config files, one per switch, edited by hand
One fixed config, pasted onto every switch
check.why: A template keeps the shared parts in one place, so a fix is made once, while each site's variables fill the blanks. Forty hand-edited files drift apart, and one fixed config would give every switch the same hostname.

Playbooks handle **upgrades** too.

Good automation is **idempotent**: running it again changes only what differs.

steps.say: Someone fixes an outage at 2 a.m. by hand. Now the running config differs from the files: **configuration drift**. A **compliance** check compares every device with the files and reports or reverses drift. Good automation is **idempotent**: running it again changes only what differs.

check.prompt: Yesterday a playbook changed 12 switches. Nobody has touched them since, and it runs again today. How many does it change?
check.answer: None: they already match the files
wrong: The same 12 again
All of them, to be safe
check.why: An idempotent task checks the current state first and acts only on differences, so a second run with nothing changed does nothing. That is what makes it safe to run on a schedule as a compliance check.

check.why: Git identifies the conflict but leaves the decision to a person, who edits the file to the intended config, removes the marker lines, and commits the result. Review catches the cases where both edits were partly right.

outro: First, a script must change one setting on one interface and leave the rest alone. Choose the HTTP method that fits best.

question: A script must change only the description of one existing interface through a device's REST API, leaving its other settings as they are. Which HTTP method fits best?
correct: PATCH
incorrect: PUT
POST
GET
feedback: PATCH changes part of an existing resource. PUT replaces the whole resource with what is sent, so leaving out the other settings could wipe them; POST creates a new resource; and GET only reads.

question: Which statements about REST, SOAP and GraphQL are accurate?
correct: SOAP messages are XML documents carried inside an envelope
A GraphQL client names exactly which fields it wants back
incorrect: GraphQL needs a separate URL for each kind of object
REST servers keep each client's session state between calls
SOAP is the newest of the three and replies in JSON
feedback: SOAP wraps XML in an envelope and checks it against a formal contract. GraphQL uses one endpoint, and the query names the fields to return. It is REST that gives each resource its own URL, and REST requests are stateless, each standing alone. SOAP is the oldest of the three, and XML is its format.

question: Aria Thorne's team must upgrade the OS on 300 access switches, and new switches are added every week. Which practices belong in the automated approach?
correct: Build the switch list at run time from the IPAM as a dynamic inventory
Write the steps once as a playbook and run it a batch at a time
Verify each image's hash, and check each switch before and after reload
incorrect: Keep a spreadsheet of switch addresses and edit it before each run
Upgrade every switch in one run so their versions stay consistent
feedback: A dynamic inventory picks up this week's new switches without anyone editing a list, which a spreadsheet will not. A playbook makes every upgrade identical, and running it in batches with a hash check and checks before and after means one bad image stops a batch, not the whole network. Upgrading everything at once turns a single faulty image into a site-wide outage.

question:
Silverkeep's nightly compliance job reports:

switch-14   NON-COMPLIANT
+ snmp-server community public RO
  (present on the device, absent from the repository)

What has MOST likely happened?
correct: Someone changed the switch by hand, outside the code: configuration drift
incorrect: Two branches changed the same line, and Git recorded the clash as a merge conflict
The dynamic inventory missed switch-14, so the job skipped it
The playbook is not idempotent, so it added the line on its last run
feedback: The line is on the device but in none of the files, so it was added outside the code: drift. A merge conflict happens in the repository, not on a device, and the job clearly reached switch-14 since it reported on it. A playbook applies only what the files say, so it could not add a line the files lack. Remove the line, since a public SNMP community is a known weakness, or add it through a reviewed commit if it is truly wanted.

question: Brom's branch and the main branch both changed the same line of the same switch config. When he merges, Git stops and marks the clash in the file for a person to settle. That clash is called a merge ___.
correct: conflict
feedback: Git combines changes to different lines on its own, but when two branches edit the same lines it identifies a conflict, marks both versions between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, and waits for a person to choose. Small branches that are merged often keep conflicts rare.

question: Brom is changing a VLAN name in the network's IaC repository. Arrange his workflow, from first to last.
items: Pull the latest main branch from the central repository
Create a branch for the change
Edit the file and commit it with a clear message
Push the branch and open a merge request for review
Merge into main once the review is approved
feedback: Starting from the latest main avoids building on stale files. The branch keeps the change away from main until it is reviewed; the commit records who changed what and why; pushing puts the branch in the central repository where others can review it; and only an approved merge reaches main, which the automation then applies.

question: Brom is in his clone of the central repository, on the main branch. Write the one git command that creates a new branch named vlan30 and switches to it.
correct: git checkout -b vlan30
git switch -c vlan30
git switch --create vlan30
git checkout -b vlan30 main
git switch -c vlan30 main
feedback: git checkout -b vlan30, or git switch -c vlan30 in newer Git, creates the branch at the current commit and moves onto it in one step. git branch vlan30 would only create it, leaving him on main, where his next commit would land.

question: NPC: What does Zero Trust actually change?
intro: I'm Val, the Ward-Smith. For years the hard part was getting past the firewall; once a laptop was on the LAN, it could reach almost everything. So one stolen laptop, plugged in at a quiet desk, could open every door in the building. Zero Trust was built to stop exactly that, so let's start with the one thing it refuses to assume.

beats.say: **Zero Trust** grants no trust for being inside the network.
Every request, from the office or a café, is authenticated and authorized before it reaches anything.

steps.say: **Zero Trust** grants no trust for being inside the network. Every request, from the office or a café, is authenticated and authorized before it reaches anything.

beats.say: **Policy-based authentication** means policy decides how strongly to check.
A password and MFA suit the wiki; an admin console needs a hardware security key.
**Authorization** is decided per request and per resource.

steps.say: **Policy-based authentication** means policy decides how strongly to check. A password and MFA suit the wiki; an admin console needs a hardware security key. **Authorization** is decided per request and per resource.

beats.say: A **policy engine** makes the decision.
A **policy enforcement point**, a gateway in front of the application, allows or blocks the request.

steps.say: A **policy engine** makes the decision. A **policy enforcement point**, a gateway in front of the application, allows or blocks the request.

check.prompt: A user passed MFA this morning. At noon she opens the HR portal's admin page. What does Zero Trust do with that request?
check.answer: Checks it against policy before letting it through
wrong: Allows it: she already signed in today
Allows it: her laptop is on the office LAN
check.why: Each request is judged when it is made. The earlier sign-in is one input, but the admin page may demand stronger authentication, and her device and context are checked again.

beats.say: **Context-aware policies** weigh more than who you are.

beats.code:
context checked
device health
location
time of day
how unusual the request is

beats.say: The device's health is its **posture**, and **EDR** is the software on it that watches for attacks.
So the same user gets different answers:

beats.code:
managed laptop  allow
new country     MFA again
unmanaged phone refuse

steps.say: **Context-aware policies** weigh more than who you are. The device's health is its **posture**, and **EDR** is the software on it that watches for attacks. So the same user gets different answers:

beats.say: **Least privileged network access** gives each user only the applications they need, not the whole network.
A VPN that drops a user onto the whole LAN is the opposite.
A **microtunnel** is a separate encrypted tunnel to one application, so the rest of the network is not even visible.

steps.say: **Least privileged network access** gives each user only the applications they need, not the whole network. A VPN that drops a user onto the whole LAN is the opposite. A **microtunnel** is a separate encrypted tunnel to one application, so the rest of the network is not even visible.

check.prompt: A contractor's laptop is infected after he connects. He has a microtunnel to the ticket system only. What can the malware reach?
check.answer: Only the ticket system, through that one tunnel
wrong: Every host on the ticket system's subnet
Whatever the VPN concentrator can route to
check.why: Microtunnels connect a device to named applications, not to subnets, so lateral movement has nowhere to go. A network-level VPN would have handed the malware the whole subnet.

beats.say: No single product does all this.
**Integrated solutions** feed their signals to one policy engine.

beats.code:
signals into one engine
identity provider
device management, EDR
access gateways
monitoring tools

beats.say: When EDR flags a laptop, that laptop's next request is refused everywhere at once.

steps.say: No single product does all this. **Integrated solutions** feed their signals to one policy engine. When EDR flags a laptop, that laptop's next request is refused everywhere at once.

outro: Next comes a list of statements about access. Pick every one that is a Zero Trust principle.

question: Which of the following are Zero Trust principles?
correct: Authenticate and authorize every request, wherever it comes from
Let policy set how strongly to authenticate, such as a key for admin consoles
Grant access to specific applications rather than to whole networks
Feed identity, device and monitoring signals into one policy engine
incorrect: Trust devices once they are plugged into the internal LAN
Authorize each user once at sign-in for the rest of the day
feedback: Zero Trust judges every request on its own merits, with authentication strength set by policy and access granted to applications, not networks. Its parts are integrated so one policy engine sees identity, device health and alerts together. Location on the LAN earns nothing, and a morning sign-in does not authorize the afternoon's requests.

question: Mira Sollen's laptop requests the payroll application in a Zero Trust design. Arrange what happens, from first to last.
items: The laptop sends a request for the payroll application
The enforcement point holds it and asks the policy engine
The policy engine checks identity, MFA, device health and context
The engine answers allow, and a tunnel opens to payroll only
feedback: The enforcement point intercepts every request; it decides nothing itself but asks the policy engine, which weighs identity, authentication strength, device posture and context. Only after an allow does the enforcement point connect the device, and only to that one application.

question: Lyra Vex is replacing a VPN that gives contractors an address on the server subnet. Each contractor should reach only the two applications they support, through separate encrypted connections, with the rest of the network invisible. Which Zero Trust approach is she describing?
correct: Least privileged access through per-application microtunnels
incorrect: A context-aware policy that admits contractors in business hours
Policy-based authentication with a stronger MFA method
A DMZ that holds the two applications for the contractors
feedback: Per-application microtunnels are how Zero Trust network access delivers least privilege: each contractor connects to named applications, and nothing else on the network is reachable or even visible. Time-of-day context and stronger MFA change who gets in, not how much they can reach, and a DMZ is a zone for public-facing servers, not a per-user access method.

question:
Lyra Vex reviews this access log entry:

user=mira.sollen app=payroll-admin mfa=passed
device=personal-tablet managed=no geo=new-country
decision=DENY reason=device-posture

Why was a user with valid credentials and MFA refused?
correct: A context-aware policy also requires a managed, healthy device
incorrect: Her MFA result was cached from an earlier session, so it was rejected
Least privilege bars every user from payroll-admin
The payroll application sits in a DMZ that blocks staff
feedback: The reason field says device posture: a context-aware policy weighed the unmanaged tablet, and the new country, against what payroll administration demands, and identity alone was not enough. The log shows MFA passed on this request, least privilege grants named users the apps they need rather than barring everyone, and nothing here involves a DMZ.

question: After two racks move onto a new VXLAN overlay, Brom reports that pings between VMs in the same segment work and small web pages load, but large file copies between the racks stall. The underlay interfaces are set to an MTU of 1500. What is the MOST likely cause?
correct: The 50-byte VXLAN wrapper pushes full-size frames past the underlay MTU
incorrect: The two VTEPs use different VNIs, which splits the segment in two
The underlay firewall blocks UDP port 4789 between the two racks
The VMs need an 802.1Q trunk to reach VMs in the other rack
feedback: Small packets still fit inside 1,500 bytes with 50 bytes of wrapping; full-size 1,500-byte packets become 1,550 and are fragmented or dropped. Raise the underlay MTU to at least 1,550, in practice to jumbo frames. Mismatched VNIs or a blocked UDP 4789 would stop every packet, pings included, and an 802.1Q trunk is what VXLAN replaces across the routed underlay.

question: Zinna Arc must let each of {{n}} VPCs reach every other privately. Peering is non-transitive, so with peering alone she needs a full mesh of peerings; with a transit gateway she needs one attachment per VPC. How many more connections does the peering design need than the transit design?
feedback_template: A full mesh of {{n}} VPCs needs {{n}} × {{others}} ÷ 2, or {{mesh}}, peerings, because no VPC forwards for another. The transit gateway is a hub, so it needs {{n}} attachments. The difference is {{expected}}, and it widens quickly as VPCs are added, which is why large cloud environments use a hub.

question: Silverkeep is connecting its data center to its cloud. Production replication needs steady latency and must stay off the internet; a backup path must be cheap, quick to set up and encrypted; and the web VPC must reach the database VPC privately. Which choices meet these requirements?
correct: A cloud interconnect for production replication
A site-to-site IPsec VPN as the backup path
A peering connection between the web and database VPCs
incorrect: A site-to-site VPN for production replication
A peering connection from the data center to the web VPC
A second cloud interconnect as the backup path
feedback: The interconnect is private and steady, which suits production. A VPN is cheap, quick and encrypted, which suits the backup path, but it rides the internet, so it cannot carry production here. Peering joins two VPCs, not a data center to a VPC. A second interconnect would work, but it fails cheap and quick: circuits cost more and can take weeks to set up.

question: Before starting a new change, Brom finds that his clone's main branch is behind the central repository. He is on main and has made no commits of his own. Write the git command that fetches the new commits from main on the remote named origin and brings them into his branch.
correct: git pull origin main
git pull
git pull --ff-only origin main
git pull --ff-only
feedback: git pull origin main fetches main's new commits from the central repository and merges them into the current branch; with no local commits of his own, that is a simple fast-forward. Plain git pull does the same when main already tracks origin/main. Starting each change from an up-to-date main is what keeps later merges small and conflicts rare.
